court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: Ejectment/assignee procedure over village-tract land under Code Civ. Proc. sec. 1526; the 'leasing' referenced is Bennett's five-year privilege to lease village-tract land from Purdy, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling or rooms. No bearing on lodging/boarding doctrine.

holding_summary: The court held that a receipt stating the term of hiring and letting was for one month only, expiring at a fixed date, created a tenancy from month to month, which either party could terminate at the end of any month without notice.

quotes.text: It being expressly understood between us, the tenant and agent, or landlord mentioned in this receipt, that this term of hiring and letting is for one month only, and will expire as aforesaid.
It is very clear that the tenancy of the intestate was from month to month. Neither party was bound to give any notice to the other in order to terminate the tenancy at the expiration of any month.

notes: who_was_letting left unclear: record shows plaintiff let 'second floor rooms' of a house to a long-term occupant but does not state whether plaintiff himself resided on another floor (householder) or was a pure rental-property owner (commercial_operator).

holding_summary: The court reaffirmed that a landlord who had let rooms (with board) to a tenant who then breached and abandoned the arrangement could not recover the full stipulated price to the end of the term, but only the damages directly resulting from the breach, because the landlord was obliged to re-let to other lodgers rather than let the rooms stand idle.

quotes.text: The Supreme Court in this State, in a case very similar to this, many years ago decided, that a landlord who had let rooms, was not entitled as matter of course to recover from the tenant who had violated his contract, and abandoned the rooms, the whole price stipulated to be paid for the use of the rooms, to the end of the period specified in the contract, but only for such damages as had directly and necessarily resulted from the breach of the contract, and that the plaintiff could not refuse to rent the rooms to other lodgers, leaving them idle, and then recover against the defendant, as for use and occupation; that although one party was chargeable with a breach .of the contract, the other party had no right to conduct himself in such a manner as to make the damages unnecessarily burdensome.

notes: Arrangement was rooms plus board for testator's family at $150/week over roughly eight months, consistent with a boardinghouse-scale operation; coded commercial_operator though a householder reading is not impossible.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: The court held that whether the relation between the parties was that of innkeeper and guest or boardinghouse keeper and boarder, the defendant was entitled to a lien on the property of the guest/boarder's employer for the unpaid balance of weekly entertainment charges.

quotes.text: If, however, their relation was that of boardinghouse keeper and boarder, the result, for two reasons, would not be changed or the judgment reversed.
The essential fact is the lien. Whether it be of the one kind or another is quite immaterial, and the variance should be disregarded.

notes: characterization left null: the court expressly declined to decide whether the relation was innkeeping or boardinghouse keeping, holding the distinction immaterial to the lien outcome. Coded favorable as an enforcement of a boarder arrangement's associated commercial remedy (lien) for weekly charges.
